title: Observation of the magnetic spin Hall effect in a ferromagnet
authors: Nicholas Davey-García, Jone Mencos, Luciano Bravo, Inge Groen, Luis E. Hueso, Andreas Berger, Fèlix Casanova
abstract: The conventional spin Hall effect generates spin currents whose flow direction, spin polarization, and driving electric field are mutually perpendicular. Magnetic order lifts this symmetry restriction and enables additional time-reversal-symmetry-odd components of the spin-conductivity tensor, giving rise to the magnetic spin Hall effect (MSHE). These components also couple the generated spin polarization to the magnetic order, providing a degree of control absent in the conventional spin Hall effect. Although the MSHE has been observed in antiferromagnets, its experimental identification in conventional ferromagnets has remained elusive. Here, using a non-local lateral spin-valve geometry, we electrically identify the MSHE and its reciprocal effect in a perpendicularly magnetized Co-based multilayer. Reversal of the multilayer magnetization reverses the MSHE and magnetic inverse spin Hall signals, revealing their time-reversal-symmetry-odd character and magnetization control. By contrast, the conventional spin Hall and inverse spin Hall signals measured in the same devices remain unchanged under magnetization reversal, consistent with their time-reversal-symmetry-even character. We obtain a magnetic spin Hall angle of $θ_{\mathrm{MSH}} = (3.8 \pm 0.6)\%$, comparable in magnitude to the spin Hall angle of heavy metals commonly used in spintronic devices, such as Pt. These results establish the MSHE as a sizable, magnetically switchable spin-charge interconversion mechanism in conventional ferromagnets.
summary: This work successfully identifies the Magnetic Spin Hall Effect (MSHE) in conventional ferromagnets using a lateral spin-valve geometry. By measuring the spin signal's dependence on magnetization reversal, the authors confirmed the MSHE's unique time-reversal-symmetry-odd character. This establishes the MSHE as a sizable, magnetically switchable spin-charge conversion mechanism comparable to established heavy metal effects.
main_problem: The primary goal was to experimentally identify the Magnetic Spin Hall Effect (MSHE) in conventional ferromagnets, as its detection had been previously elusive.
main_result: The MSHE was unequivocally identified by observing that the associated spin signal reverses sign upon magnetization reversal, confirming its time-reversal-symmetry-odd character. The measured magnetic spin Hall angle was found to be $(3.8 \pm 0.6)\%$.
method: The study utilized a non-local lateral spin-valve (LSV) geometry to electrically measure spin signals, comparing the response to magnetization reversal against conventional spin Hall effects.
model_or_system: The experiment uses perpendicularly magnetized (PMA) Co-based multilayer thin films integrated into a lateral spin-valve structure, allowing for precise control and measurement of spin transport phenomena.
key_observables: Non-local resistance ($\Delta R_{NL}$), MSHE/MISHE signals, and the magnetic spin Hall angle ($	heta_{MSH}$).
important_parameters: Magnetic spin Hall angle $	heta_{\mathrm{MSH}} = (3.8 \pm 0.6)\%$; spin diffusion length $\lambda_{PMA}^{\perp} = 0.31 \pm 0.06$ nm.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the use of LSV architectures to isolate the effect and relies on theoretical models to decouple the TRS-odd (MSHE) from the TRS-even (SHE) components.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematics comparing SHE and MSHE mechanisms, and show non-local spin signal measurements ($\Delta R_{NL}$) demonstrating the sign reversal characteristic of the MSHE upon magnetization reversal.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical difference between TRS-even (SHE) and TRS-odd (MSHE) components, details the fabrication and measurement setup using LSV, and presents the key results showing the distinct magnetic switching behavior of the MSHE signal.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the ability to electrically isolate and quantify a symmetry-protected spin-charge conversion mechanism (MSHE) is highly relevant to understanding spin-orbit torque physics and spintronics, which often interfaces with quantum control concepts.
